findings.title: Experts do not disagree more where the physics of gas exchange leaves them
findings.summary: We asked whether two experts disagree about a threshold on the tests where their marks sit far from what the gas-exchange curves alone would say, as if one of them followed a habit rather than the physiology. On about 220 tests read by two or more experts, in 6 labs, the distance between the experts and a detector taught only by physics was unrelated to how far apart the experts were, for VT1 and VT2. A model trained on expert marks did err more where the experts disagreed, mostly on VT2. What makes a test ambiguous to humans is learned with the marks; it is not a split between physiology and habit. A refuted idea, recorded as a finding.
findings.method: Tests read by two or more experts, labs with at least ten such tests; per test, each detector's distance from the experts' mean mark against the spread of their marks; rank correlation within lab, pooled, with a bootstrap over tests; criteria fixed in advance.

findings.title: A detector taught only by a simulator improves by learning from real tests it labelled itself
findings.summary: We asked whether a detector that has never seen an expert's mark can get closer to the experts without anyone marking anything. The simulator-taught detector labelled every real test of the training labs; the same kind of model then learned from those real curves and its own labels. On labs it had never seen, it placed VT1 about 5 mL/min closer to the experts than its teacher, in two independent simulations, and about 15 to 20 mL/min closer than a cohort-typical guess, with no human label at all. It is still about 15 to 20 mL/min behind the current production model, which learned from thousands of expert marks. VT2 improved a little too but stays worse than the guess. Real curves carry shape the simulator lacks, and a model can pick it up from its own answers. Regraded exploratory on 2026-11-23: in two further simulations the gain was smaller (about 2 to 4 mL/min) and in one of them not clearly above zero; more rounds of self-teaching added nothing on VT1, letting a lab's own unmarked tests teach the detector did not help, and mixing its answers into a model trained on expert marks did not improve that model. The detector itself still beats the guess in every simulation.
findings.method: Teacher: gradient-boosted trees trained only on simulated tests (two new simulation seeds). Student: the same trees trained on the real tests of the training labs with the teacher's answers as labels, each lab held out in turn, three random seeds averaged; no expert label used anywhere; criteria fixed in advance, compared test by test with the teacher and with a cohort-typical guess.

findings.title: A detector that never saw an expert's mark places VT1 better than a cohort-typical guess
findings.summary: We asked whether simulated tests, whose thresholds are known because a simple model of the exercising body writes them, can teach a detector anything about real tests. A tree model trained only on 4,000 simulated tests, with no human label at all, placed VT1 about 10 mL/min closer to the experts than a cohort-typical guess, across labs it had never seen, and was better in 8 of 12 labs. It did best in labs where models trained on expert marks do worst, and worst in others: the simulator defines VT1 as a change of slope, so where it lands shows how far each lab's marking sits from that definition. It did not place VT2 better than the guess. Adding the simulated tests to real labelled ones did not help, with few labels or many. Regraded robust on 2026-11-22: two further, independent simulations gave the same result (about 10 to 15 mL/min better than the guess on VT1, worse on VT2), and a simulation four times larger gained only a few mL/min.
findings.method: A parametric simulator of incremental tests with a widened population (fitness, sampling, duration, slopes, transition widths and noise varied); gradient-boosted trees on the same binned signals as the real-data models, three random seeds averaged; each real lab scored as unseen; criteria fixed in advance, compared test by test with a cohort-typical guess and with the same trees trained on real labels.

findings.title: Most of a person's VO2max is already written in the submaximal response
findings.summary: We asked whether a test stopped early, at an objective submaximal point, still tells the person's ceiling. Stopped when the respiratory exchange ratio first holds 1.00, about three minutes before the usual end and at about 85% of the peak oxygen uptake, a small tree model predicted VO2max to within about 290 mL/min, roughly 10% of a typical value, against about 1,500 mL/min for a cohort-typical guess and about 340 mL/min for a simple proportion of the oxygen uptake at the stop. Stopping earlier, at 0.95, lost accuracy (about 400 mL/min); stopping later, at 1.05, gained it (about 210 mL/min). The last minutes of the curves added nothing beyond a handful of numbers read at the stop, and in the most regular labs the simple proportion was as good as the model. A shorter, safer test may be enough to estimate fitness. Checked again on 2026-11-20 without one lab whose units did not match: the model still beat the simple proportion by about 70 mL/min, in 8 of 11 labs. It needs most of the labelled tests: with 400 it was about 15 mL/min worse, with 100 about 110 worse.
findings.method: Each test cut where its smoothed exchange ratio first held a set level for 30 seconds; gradient-boosted trees on 14 numbers at the cut, alone and with the last six minutes of six signals; each lab held out in turn, three random seeds averaged; criteria fixed in advance, compared test by test with a cohort-typical guess and a proportional rule fitted on the training labs only.

findings.title: Recovery after the peak does not carry where the thresholds were
findings.summary: We asked whether the first five minutes after peak exercise remember where VT1 and VT2 sat on the ramp, which would make the thresholds a property of the whole response rather than of a moment. They do not. A tree model reading recovery alone placed VT1 about 15 mL/min further from the experts than a cohort-typical guess, and VT2 no better. Adding recovery to the ramp changed neither threshold by more than a few mL/min, in either direction. Only about a quarter of tests record two minutes of recovery, which weakens the test, but where recovery was present the model could use it and found nothing. The thresholds are read from the ramp.
findings.method: Gradient-boosted trees on six signals over the first five minutes after the peak, each divided by its value at the peak, alone and added to the ramp's signals; each lab held out in turn, three random seeds averaged; criteria fixed in advance, compared test by test with a cohort-typical guess and with the same trees on the ramp alone.

findings.title: Near VT1, breathing does not switch between two patterns
findings.summary: Breath-to-breath ventilation grows more variable around VT1. One reading was that people alternate between deep, slow breaths and shallow, fast ones as the threshold nears. We tested it on almost a thousand breath-by-breath tests: breathing is no more two-patterned at the experts' VT1 than elsewhere. It is most two-patterned about two minutes before VT1 and becomes steadily less so after. Used to place VT1 without labels, it did worse than a cohort-typical guess. The extra variability near VT1 is larger breaths, not switching.
findings.method: Per breath, tidal volume and breathing frequency relative to their running medians, projected on a deep-and-slow axis; a bimodality coefficient in moving windows, averaged on the experts' VT1 marks against marks placed at random, and read as a label-free detector scored with each lab held out; nothing fitted; criteria fixed in advance.

findings.title: Teaching the network to fill in hidden stretches of the curves, without labels, makes it worse at placing VT1
findings.summary: Before learning from labels, the small network first learned to fill in hidden stretches of each test's curves from the rest. It then placed VT1 about 7 mL/min further from the experts than the same network without this step, did not help with only 400 labelled tests, and did not help the average with the tree model. Letting it also see the new lab's curves, never their labels, did not help either. Filling in gaps rewards the smooth trend of a test, which the tree model already reads, not the bends where a threshold sits. This kind of label-free learning is dropped on this data; the average of network and trees remains the best way found to place VT1.
findings.method: Convolutional network on every signal along the test's VO2 axis, first trained without labels to reconstruct three hidden stretches per test, then on labels; each lab held out in turn, three random seeds averaged, at all data and at two random samples of 400 labelled tests, once also pretrained on the held-out lab's unlabelled curves; criteria fixed in advance, compared test by test with the same network without pretraining.

findings.title: Averaging a shape-reading network with the tree model places VT1 better than the current production model, most of all with few labels
findings.summary: Averaging the answers of the small network that reads the curves' shape and of the tree model placed VT1 about 15 mL/min closer to the experts than the current production model, in four separate sets of random seeds, although neither model had seen the test's lab and the production model had seen most of them. VT2 was level. Against the tree model alone the average was better by 4 to 8 mL/min in every set, and clearly so in two of the three fresh sets, which met the bar fixed in advance (checked again on 2026-11-19). The gain is small, and it held even when the network on its own was at its weakest, so it comes from the two models making different mistakes. With only 400 labelled tests the average beat the tree model trained on the same tests by about 10 mL/min on VT1 and 5 on VT2, which matters for a product that must learn from few labelled tests. A network with half the filters did just as well.
findings.method: Convolutional network and gradient-boosted trees on every signal along the test's VO2 axis, each lab held out in turn, three random seeds averaged per network, three fresh sets of seeds at all data, two random samples of 400 labelled tests and one of 800, and a narrower network; averaged with equal weight, fixed in advance, and compared test by test with the tree model and the production model.

findings.title: Where a bend sits on the test matters: re-reading tests on cropped ranges makes the network worse
findings.summary: Showing the small network a fresh random crop of each test's VO2 range at every pass, with the threshold moved along, made it about 15 mL/min worse on VT1 and 10 on VT2 than the same network trained on whole tests, and it did not help with 400 or 800 labelled tests. A threshold is not only a bend in the curves wherever it happens: where along the test's range the bend falls carries information that cropping destroys. Averaged over three random seeds, the uncropped network is level with the tree model on VT1 and behind it on VT2. Averaging the network's and the tree model's answers placed VT1 closer to the experts than either alone, and closer than the current production model, though neither model saw the test's lab; this was noticed after the fact, so it is a lead now being repeated with fresh seeds, not yet a result.
findings.method: Convolutional network on every signal along the test's VO2 axis, each lab held out in turn, three random seeds averaged, with and without random crops, at all data and at 400 and 800 labelled tests; compared test by test with the tree model and the production model.

findings.title: A small network that reads the shape of the curves does worse than the tree model, for lack of data
findings.summary: A small convolutional network, which slides the same short filters along the VO2 axis so that a bend in the curves is recognised wherever it happens, was about 20 mL/min worse than the tree model on VT1 and about 25 worse on VT2, and on VT2 it did not beat a cohort-typical guess. It was also behind the current production model on both thresholds. With 400 or 800 labelled tests it stayed 13 to 21 mL/min behind the trees on VT1. A version with a quarter of the parameters did no worse, which points to too few labelled tests for its size rather than too little capacity. It is an eighth of the size of the tree model and trains in about a minute. Next, the same network is shown many re-readings of each test (random crops of its VO2 range), a way to stretch the labels already there.
findings.method: Convolutional network on every signal along the test's VO2 axis, each lab held out in turn, one random seed on all data, two random samples of 400 labelled tests, one of 800, and a narrower version, compared with the tree model and the production model on the same tests.

findings.title: Asking each point of the test whether the threshold is passed does worse than reading the whole test
findings.summary: A model that judged every point along the VO2 axis, through a short window of every signal, as before or after the threshold, and placed the threshold where its answer turned, was about 20 mL/min worse on VT1 and 15 on VT2 than the tree model that reads the whole test at once. It still beat a cohort-typical guess, and in four of the labs where experts disagree most it beat the current production model on VT1, but in two labs it was off by hundreds. It did not help with only 400 labelled tests, and it did better with 400 than with all of them, a sign that its read-out is unstable: one early false 'passed' locks in. Next is a small network that reads the shape of the curves anywhere along the test.
findings.method: Gradient-boosted classifier on every point of each test, each lab held out in turn, one random seed on all data and two random samples of 400 labelled tests, compared with the tree model and the production model on the same tests.

findings.title: The tree model is already the size its labels support
findings.summary: A model six times larger was level with the usual one on VT1 and about 5 mL/min worse on VT2, at five times the training time. A sixth of the size lost about 10 mL/min on VT1, and a twentieth lost about 30 on VT1 and 7 on VT2, though both still beat a cohort-typical guess. With only 400 labelled tests the smaller model was about 2 mL/min better on VT2 in both random samples of tests, but on VT1 it was level in one sample and slightly worse in the other. More capacity buys nothing without more or different information, so the next gains must come from a different method or different inputs, not a bigger or smaller version of this one.
findings.method: Gradient-boosted trees at three sizes, each lab held out in turn, compared test by test with the usual size over the same random seeds, and at 400 labelled tests sampled twice.

findings.title: A four-signal model is nearly as good, but not shown equal, and needs no fewer labels
findings.summary: Repeated with fresh random seeds, the model that reads only four signals stayed within about 2 mL/min of the full model on both thresholds, at a third of the input and about half the training time. In each repeat one threshold's uncertainty still reached just past the margin fixed in advance, so it is not called as good. With 400 labelled tests it was level with the full model, and with 800 it fell behind on VT1 by about 5 mL/min: fewer signals do not let the model learn from fewer labels. The lead is closed.
findings.method: Gradient-boosted trees, each lab held out in turn, compared test by test with the same model on all signals, over two sets of random seeds and at two smaller numbers of labelled tests drawn twice each.

findings.title: VT1 rests on a small group of signals; VT2 is spread wider
findings.summary: Removing four signals together raises the VT1 error by about 14 mL/min and the VT2 error by about 5, although removing any one of them alone changed little. A model that reads only those four signals, a third of the input, comes within about 1 mL/min of the full model on both thresholds, but the uncertainty on VT1 is still slightly too wide to call it as good. One signal alone is clearly worse, yet still better than a cohort-typical guess.
findings.method: Gradient-boosted trees retrained on three groups of signals, each lab held out in turn, compared test by test with the same model on all signals; the four signals were chosen from the previous single-signal experiment.

findings.title: No single signal carries either threshold
findings.summary: Removing any one of the thirteen signals a simple model reads moves its VT1 error by at most about 6 mL/min and its VT2 error by at most about 2. Only one signal is clearly needed for VT1, and none for VT2. Removing signals one at a time hides what they do together: see the finding on groups of signals.
findings.method: Gradient-boosted trees retrained thirteen times, each time without one signal, each lab held out in turn, compared test by test with the same model on all signals.

findings.title: Smoothing the signals more or less does not place exercise start better
findings.summary: The current production rule smooths the signals before it looks for the start of exercise and of recovery. Making that smoothing three times shorter, twice or four times longer did not place either boundary closer to the expert's mark; longer smoothing put recovery start later than it should, by 4 to 9 seconds. The rare large misses at exercise start come from somewhere else.
findings.method: Four smoothing settings compared recording by recording with the default on 45 recordings whose start of exercise and recovery an expert marked; tuned and scored on the same recordings.

findings.title: More labels of the same kind stop helping VT2 at about 1,500 tests
findings.summary: A simple model stops improving on VT2 somewhere between 1,200 and 1,600 expert-labelled tests: beyond that, adding more tests of the same kind changes nothing measurable. VT1 is at or just short of the same point by 1,600, with a few mL/min left at most. Below about 1,200 tests, which tests are labelled matters almost as much as how many. Further progress has to come from what the model sees, or from the many recordings nobody labelled, not from more labels.
findings.method: Gradient-boosted trees trained on 1,200 and 1,600 tests picked at random, each lab held out in turn, compared test by test with the same model trained on all tests; three independent random picks agree.

findings.title: A few hundred labelled tests are enough to beat a cohort-typical guess
findings.summary: Trained on a random 100 to 200 expert-labelled tests from other labs, a simple model already places VT1 closer to the experts than a cohort-typical guess on labs it never saw; VT2 needs about 200 to 400. With 800 labelled tests it matches the current production model on VT1. It keeps improving beyond 800 tests, by a few mL/min.
findings.method: Gradient-boosted trees trained on 50 to 800 tests picked at random, each lab held out in turn, compared test by test with the same model trained on all tests; two independent random picks agree on both thresholds.

findings.title: On VT1, a simple model from other labs beats the current production model
findings.summary: Compared test by test, the research model places VT1 about 10 mL/min closer to the experts than the current production model, and is better in 7 of 12 labs, although it never saw any of them and the production model had seen most. On VT2 the two are level. Averaging the two models' answers brought VT2 a few mL/min closer than either alone, a lead still to test on models that never saw the test's lab.
findings.method: The same held-out tests scored by both models, each lab held out in turn; the uncertainty range of the per-test difference, from resampling whole recordings within each lab, stays below zero on VT1 and crosses zero on VT2.

findings.title: A model trained on other labs carries to a new one
findings.summary: A simple model trained only on other labs, given each test's ventilation and gas-exchange signals on a common intensity axis, places VT1 about 40 mL/min and VT2 about 20 mL/min closer to the experts than a cohort-typical guess, on labs it never saw. It holds in 10 or 11 of the 12 labs, cycling and running, clinical and athletic, and matches the current production model without having seen any of those labs.
findings.method: Gradient-boosted trees; each lab held out in turn; three random seeds, which agree within 2 mL/min; the gain's uncertainty range stays clear of zero on both thresholds.

findings.title: On treadmill tests, the research model halves the production model's VT1 error
findings.summary: Split by how a test was run, the research model's VT1 error on treadmill tests is about 170 mL/min, against about 330 for the current production model and 470 for a cohort-typical guess. On cycle ergometers the two models are level. It is a split looked at after the fact, on few treadmill tests, so it is a lead to test on its own, not yet a result.
findings.method: Errors from the held-out predictions of the three-seed model, grouped by the ergometer recorded in each test's load channel.

findings.title: Experts disagree, and how much depends on the lab
findings.summary: When two experts mark the same test, their VT1 readings sit about 90 to 340 mL/min apart depending on the lab, and their VT2 readings about 70 to 220. A model that found the true threshold would still sit roughly 0.7 times that gap from each expert, so that floor, not zero, is what a model is judged against.
findings.method: Tests read independently by several experts, in six labs: the mean gap between two readings of the same test.

findings.title: Textbook breakpoints corroborate; they do not detect
findings.summary: Run automatically over the exercise phase, the classical V-slope and ventilatory-equivalent breakpoints place both thresholds further from the experts than a cohort-typical guess. They are worth showing beside a result, as evidence to inspect, not as the answer.
findings.method: No tuning; scored on the same tests and in the same way as the models.

findings.title: A model is only as good as the signal it is handed
findings.summary: Given breath-by-breath rows instead of the one-second series it was built on, the current production model placed VT2 about 40 mL/min further from the experts. The service already resamples every upload, so users were never affected. Every model is now measured exactly as production feeds it.
findings.method: The same model and tests, scored through both inputs.

findings.title: One benchmark for every idea
findings.summary: Every result is measured the same way: on labs a model never trained on, against a cohort-typical guess, the current production model and the gap between experts. The benchmark reproduces our earlier reference figures exactly, so old and new numbers compare.
findings.method: Twelve labs, each held out in turn; two more sealed for final checks; uncertainty from resampling whole recordings within each lab.

timeline.title: Research and production models averaged
timeline.outcome: A small VT2 gain, kept as a lead: half of the average had seen the test labs.

timeline.title: Research model against production, test by test
timeline.outcome: Better on VT1, level on VT2.

timeline.title: Tree model, three seeds
timeline.outcome: Held under resampling: the transfer result became robust.

timeline.title: Production model re-measured through its own input
timeline.outcome: Overturned an earlier result, now corrected.

timeline.title: Tree model on binned signals
timeline.outcome: Beat a cohort-typical guess on every threshold, on unseen labs.

corrections.text: From one random seed we wrote that the small network was about 20 mL/min worse than the tree model on VT1 and did not beat a cohort-typical guess on VT2. Averaged over three seeds it is level with the trees on VT1 and does beat the guess on VT2, though it stays behind the trees there. One seed of this network is not enough to judge it.

After removing signals one at a time, we wrote that the model spreads what it uses across signals that stand in for each other. For VT1 that overstated it: removing four signals together raises the VT1 error by about 14 mL/min. The finding now says VT1 rests on a small group of signals.

An early run reported the production model as worse than a cohort-typical guess on VT2. The benchmark had handed it the wrong input. Re-measured the same day, it is better, and the claim was withdrawn before anyone relied on it.
